title: Autumn in the High Tatras
blurb: From 42 kilometers in Berlin to an unscripted journey through historic Wrocław and the misty alpine ridges and glacial lakes of the High Tatras.

entries.label: Portfolio
entries.title: Selected Photographs
text: Five of my favorite photographs from two weeks traveling across Germany, Poland, and Slovakia. The day-by-day diary begins below.

entries.label: Prologue · Sep 27
entries.title: 2026 Berlin Marathon
text: After a quick layover in Zurich to shake out my legs, I arrived in Berlin two days before the race with a slim itinerary. A Polish friend from my run club had pitched the idea of exploring Poland after running 26.2 miles. The only things booked were my hotel in Berlin and a return flight from Kraków.

A serious training cycle never really materialized for this race. Managing an injury, I was running only a few days a week on low mileage, but on race morning conditions were ideal at 55 degrees and sunny. My heart rate stayed low around 145 bpm, but within the first couple miles I could already tell my legs were heavy. I knew what was coming, and I kept repeating the same phrase in my head: "this is just going to be a mechanical bottleneck." Sure enough, right past mile twenty, the breakdown arrived. The final miles turned into pure damage control, but I held things together down Unter den Linden and crossed beneath the Brandenburg Gate in 2:50:58.

I checked out of my hotel on Monday morning, spent an extra night in Alexanderplatz exploring the East Side Gallery, and booked the rest of my stays across Poland on the fly. On Tuesday morning, with twenty-six race miles in my legs, I boarded a regional train to Wrocław to begin a few days in the city before heading south to the High Tatras.

entries.label: Day 1 · Sep 29
entries.title: Arrival in Wrocław & Neon Courtyard
text: The train rolled east across the German-Polish border, dropping me at Wrocław Główny. It was my first time in Poland, and stepping into the historic railway terminal felt like entering an entirely different chapter of the trip. I hopped on the 18 tram to my hotel, dropped my bags, and walked out into the late afternoon sun through the cobblestone streets toward the Rynek.

For dinner, I stopped at a vegan ramen spot for crispy mushroom katsu ramen and vegan ribs. Afterward, I walked around the corner to Ruska 46, a hidden courtyard known as the Neon Side Gallery. During the Cold War, Wrocław was famous for its neon signs. A local foundation rescued dozens of them from old cinemas, hotels, and train stations and mounted them across the tenement walls. The dark brick courtyard glowed in electric blues, reds, and yellows. It was a great welcome to the city.

entries.label: Day 2 · Sep 30
entries.title: Wrocław Historic Islands & Cathedral
text: I started the morning with Turkish eggs, then walked over to the White Stork Synagogue. I spent time reading through the exhibits on the history of Jews in Wrocław, tracing the alternating waves of prosperity and backlash they faced over the centuries. From there, I took the tram east to Szczytnicki Park. I walked the quiet paths through the northern woods first before heading down toward Centennial Hall. I caught the Pergola fountain show on the hour and strolled through the Japanese Garden. For lunch along the river, I ordered the ruskie and the sweet apple pie pierogi, which ended up setting the bar for dumplings for the entire trip.

In the late afternoon, I climbed the towers of St. Mary Magdalene to reach the Witches' Bridge, a narrow footbridge suspended forty-five meters high between the spires. Along the climb, speakers played eerie sounds while displays told the local folklore of Tekla, a vain girl condemned to sweep the walkway forever until a kind young witch named Martynka flew up on her broom to free her. Out on the bridge, miniature bronze statues of the two sat perched on the railing as the view opened across the entire city. Toward the end of sunset, a travel YouTuber stepped out to vlog, visibly nervous about the height. When I showed him a few frames on my camera screen, he asked if I was a professional.

The sky just kept getting better as the light dropped. The golden sunset faded into deep layers of orange and violet. Twenty-nine minutes after the sun dipped below the horizon, the twilight finally peaked: the streetlamps flickered on below, the clock tower lit up, and the sky turned an electric royal blue over the red-tiled roofs. I stayed on the bridge soaking it in until the afterglow completely vanished. Down in the street, dinner was an underwhelming plate of herring and borscht, but washed down with a cold Coke Classic, it was easy to shrug off. Back in my room, I spent the evening listening to Network Effect while booking my mountain hostels in Zakopane and Slovakia on the fly.

entries.label: Day 3 · Oct 1
entries.title: Wrocław Riverfront & Old Town
text: I started the morning with shakshuka, fresh sourdough, and a bottled kombucha. From there, I walked east along the river to Hydropolis to check out the underground water reservoir museum. Heading north into the Nadodrze neighborhood, I ducked into the Podwórko Roosevelta courtyards: an open-air alleyway covered in colorful community folk art, sculpted ceramic insects, and a giant hand-painted Shrek mural where I couldn't resist stopping for a selfie.

Heading back through the Market Square in the late afternoon, I came across a ceremony for the start of the university year. Students and faculty were gathered on the cobblestones with banners while a military band played and a choir sang. It was an energetic farewell to the city. With reports of early fresh snow on the high Tatra peaks, I spent the evening at Decathlon getting geared up. The staff warned me about icy granite on the summits, so I picked up microspikes and extra cold-weather gear. Back at my room, I finished packing and set an early alarm for the morning train south to Zakopane.

entries.label: Day 4 · Oct 2
entries.title: Sarnia Skała Loop
text: I took the direct train from Wrocław to Zakopane. I still had a few hours of daylight left before sunset. After checking into my room, I packed some waffles and gummy clusters and headed out for Sarnia Skała right from my door. The trail passed the Wielka Krokiew ski jump and climbed through autumn woods to a rocky outcrop. From the top, I got my first look at the snow-covered high peaks and Mount Giewont in the late afternoon sun.

On the way down, I slipped on the slick, polished limestone and cut my finger. Once I finished the loop, I walked into town and stopped at an apteka for bandages. The bistro I wanted for dinner was already closed, and my backup meal of eight potato kopytka was nowhere near enough calories. I walked way too far looking for a second dinner before finally giving up and raiding the snacks back in my room.

entries.label: Day 5 · Oct 3
entries.title: Valley of the Five Lakes & Morskie Oko
text: My aparthotel had no USB charger, so I drained my battery pack the night before just to get my phone two-thirds charged. In the morning, I flagged down a private minivan in Zakopane to reach the trailhead. The walk up the valley was stunning from the start, and it only kept improving. Breaking into the Valley of the Five Lakes, I was blown away by the landscape: orange autumn foliage, fresh snow, gray granite, and deep green water.

I stopped at the mountain hut for a bowl of borscht. Leaving the hut, I took a wrong turn onto some ice, backtracked, and found the trail over the ridge to Morskie Oko. Along the way, I heard the first English on the trail outside of the hut staff. I asked the guy where he was from, and it turned out he was from West Virginia. We chatted as we hiked over toward the lake. I was moving well ahead of schedule, so once I reached Morskie Oko, I decided to continue past the main lake and hike up to Czarny Staw.

I had no cell reception to check what the green trail above entailed. I figured I had plenty of time and could turn back whenever I wanted. In reality, it is one of the most technical routes in the park. The hiking quickly gave way to scrambling. Near the snowline, I considered turning back, but a descending hiker told me it was silly to stop there.

I put on my microspikes and pushed higher. About two hundred meters below the saddle, the route hit a near-vertical climb requiring three points of contact. It was getting late, and knowing I am a slow downclimber, my nerves were not happy with the situation. I took a few photos and began working my way back down.

I carefully made my way back past the lakes and reached the trailhead right at six. After catching the bus back to Zakopane, my first stop was an electronics shop in town to pick up a wall charger. From there, I went to dinner and devoured both a Margherita pizza and salmon tagliatelle, followed by apple pie and ice cream.

entries.label: Day 6 · Oct 4
entries.title: Kościelisko Valley & Termy Chochołowskie
text: Kościelisko was meant to be a recovery day. I took the bus to the trailhead, planning a quick trip so I wouldn't overdo it. The route was a flat out-and-back through the valley, passing beautiful horses pulling carriages along the trail. I grabbed pancakes at the mountain hut and turned back.

Afterward, I set off for Termy Chochołowskie. I ended up catching the wrong minibus, which dropped me off in the wrong spot. I walked up the road where it left me and waited for the real bus. Once there, I spent the first hour and fifteen minutes hitting all the baths, including ten minutes each in the sulfur and brine pools. Afterward, I headed up to the saunarium and grabbed chicken teriyaki with rice noodles. On the last bus back to Zakopane, the driver suddenly stopped because a guy was sitting right in the middle of the street. A few passengers got off to help him out of the road to the guardrail and called for help before we got moving again.

entries.label: Day 7 · Oct 5
entries.title: Predné Solisko & Štrbské Pleso
text: Leaving Zakopane started with an awkward key handoff at the aparthotel, where the hosts only spoke Polish. While waiting at the stop for the bus into town, I grabbed tea with a local to pass the time. The connection into Slovakia went smoothly: a bus down to Poprad, then a local train to Štrba. On the ride over, an older Slovakian man overheard where I was from and struck up a conversation that moved through politics, Trump, and the war in Ukraine.

Getting to the hostel early left me with an open afternoon, so I asked the front desk what to do. The guy working suggested Predné Solisko. I dropped my bags, changed clothes, and took the cog railway up to Štrbské Pleso. After walking around the lake, I accidentally took the yellow trail into the woods instead of the blue. A quick check of the map showed it still connected to the summit route, so I stayed on it. The detour paid off with a great view up the valley through the pine scrub where the trails intersected. Past the top of the ski slope, the blue trail kicked into a steep, rocky grind. It was just up and up, and I had to stop for breaks along the way.

At the summit, I hung out for a while taking in the views across the surrounding peaks and valleys before starting the descent. Back at the ski slope, I stopped for my first plate of halušky, the local potato dumplings covered in sheep cheese. I then followed the blue trail down the rest of the ski slope to the bottom. Walking back around Štrbské Pleso, I realized that if I waited a little longer, I could catch the sunset. It was well worth the wait: the light turned pink, casting the Belt of Venus and the glowing ridges directly across the calm water.

entries.label: Day 8 · Oct 6
entries.title: Rysy Summit & Veľké Hincovo
text: Starting up the trail from Štrbské Pleso, I passed a group of Slovak military personnel heading out. One greeted me with a quick "dzień," which caught me off guard and left me flustered as I threw a "dzień" right back. Before committing to the main peak, I took a morning spur trail out to Veľké Hincovo pleso, the largest and deepest natural lake in Slovakia. Heading back toward the main route, I crossed paths with the soldiers again as they were descending, trading a mix of "hello" and "ahoj." Further up the valley, I passed a traditional Tatra porter methodically hauling an enormous wooden pack frame of supplies toward the summit hut.

The chain-assisted scrambles started just below Chata pod Rysmi, feeling solid and manageable on the ascent. Above the hut, after a quick bathroom break, the trail steepened through granite slabs and packed snow. I scrambled up to the Slovak peak first for an open panorama of jagged ridges that stretched far into the distance. From there, I crossed the crest to the Polish summit, standing on the country's highest point and looking thousands of feet straight down the north face into Morskie Oko.

On the descent, I stopped at the hut for parené buchty, the giant steamed sweet dumplings filled with jam. Downclimbing the chains afterward felt far freakier than going up, forcing me to take every move slowly with three points of contact on the rock. Further down, rather than picking my way across a steep snowfield, I just slid down the snow on my boots, trailing one hand for balance. Near the valley floor, I had enough time for a quick detour through the Symbolic Cemetery tucked under the cliffs at Popradské pleso. By the time I reached Štrbské Pleso, the waterside restaurant I had been eyeing was closed, but after eighteen miles on the trail, I happily settled into another spot and put away a whole trout alongside a full plate of halušky.

entries.label: Day 9 · Oct 7
entries.title: Kriváň Summit Loop
text: My plan for Kriváň was a loop: take the steep trail up to the summit and descend the longer route through Tri Studničky. I had expected an unassisted scramble, but ran into a chain-assisted section near the top. The summit was biting cold and intensely windy beside the wooden double cross. Because Kriváň sits on the western flank of the massif, the perspective is completely unique. To the west lay the rolling orange peaks of the Western Tatras, while looking east from outside the range, the entire High Tatras stood arrayed in one continuous, jagged wall.

For the descent, I took the green trail down toward Tri Studničky. Along the way, I passed a crew of trail maintenance workers and eventually noticed signs marking the route as closed, which explained why I had that entire descent to myself after sharing the summit with a crowd. Looking at my watch, I realized the timing was tight. If I wanted to catch the cog railway down, shower, and get back up to the lake for sunset, I had to move. I picked up the pace and ran the remaining five miles back toward Štrbské Pleso.

The rush paid off. I caught the cog train down to Štrba, grabbed a quick snack, chatted at the hostel, showered, and hopped the next train right back up. Reaching Štrbské Pleso just before sunset, I paused by the shore to take in the calm mirror reflections of the peaks and clouds. From there, I headed up a trail to a viewpoint west of the lake to watch the red sun sink through a thick orange haze on the horizon. I walked back down to the water hoping for another magical pink twilight like my first hike in Slovakia, but the pink never appeared. I was disappointed, but still glad I had pushed to watch the sun go down.

entries.label: Day 10 · Oct 8
entries.title: Zelené Pleso to Starý Smokovec Traverse
text: The forecast called for rain and wind gusts up to 135 km/h, so pushing for a high peak didn't make much sense. Instead, I took the train across the valley to do a lower traverse. The rain held off on the climb up to Zelené pleso, where thick clouds covered the surrounding peaks. The hut at the lake was closed for maintenance, and the wind was fierce enough to slide my water bottle across the outdoor picnic table while I wolfed down pretzels and gummy bears.

From the lake, the trail climbed steeply toward the headwall, passing a small tarn where I couldn't tell if the surface was covered in scum or frozen until I tossed a pebble and watched it skitter across the ice. The chain-assisted sections above were straightforward, offering an easy handhold to walk up the rock before switchbacking to the summit of Veľká Svišťovka. The wind gave a momentary lull before sudden, violent gusts slammed the ridge, strong enough to push you around. I handed my phone to the only other guy up there to grab a photo, but quickly gave up trying to explain how I wanted the shot framed. It was freezing and wild, and I just wanted to get off the peak.

I power-hiked the high ridge traverse across toward the ski area at Skalnaté pleso. The main lodge by the lake was shut down, but a smaller hut just down the trail was open, so I stopped for some smoked cheese and warm food. A light drizzle began falling just as I stepped back outside. Continuing along the ridge into the valley, I crossed a wooden bridge where a couple was stopped, pointing into the autumn brush at three grazing deer. A little further down the trail, I flagged down another couple so they wouldn't miss them.

Lower down, the trail followed the cascades of the Cold Water Waterfalls. I waited on a wooden footbridge for a couple to finish making out before grabbing a selfie in front of the gorge. Noticing extra viewpoints marked down a yellow spur trail, I took a look, chatted with hikers, and directed a confused tourist on the best route back to his hotel. Up around the Hrebienok resort area, I spotted a large carved wooden frog that I liked and stopped for a selfie matching its expression before finishing the walk into Starý Smokovec. After seventeen miles in the wind, I rewarded myself with sushi, dinner, and some local cakes before catching the electric train and cog railway back to the hostel.

entries.label: Day 11 · Oct 9
entries.title: Batizovské & Velické Pleso Traverse
text: The morning started with a quiet train ride to the trailhead. Unlike the crowded routes earlier in the week, I had the entire climb up the yellow trail to myself, seeing no one as the path wound through the forest. As the temperature warmed up, the valley clouds rose right along with me as I climbed, following me up the mountain all the way to Batizovské pleso.

I arrived at the lake with low visibility and shifting clouds obstructing the view, but after waiting by the shore, the clouds finally broke to reveal the peaks across the water. From there, I pushed east along the red trail toward Velické pleso. At Sliezsky Dom, I stopped for lunch and had chicken skewers, then walked a full loop around the lake to take in the waterfall tumbling down the headwall.
With an eye on the time, I started my descent down the mountain, keeping a steady pace to make sure I caught the electric train in time to connect onward to Kraków.

entries.label: Day 12 · Oct 10
entries.title: Vistula River Morning Run
text: After eight straight days in the Tatras, waking up in Kraków called for an easy, flat shakeout. I ran a 6.5-mile loop along the paved boulevards and quiet gravel paths of the Vistula River. The water was dead calm beneath the limestone bluff of Wawel Castle, shared with early morning rowing crews and dragon boaters. I looped back into Kazimierz across Father Bernatek's Footbridge beneath the suspended bronze acrobat sculptures, showered, and walked over to a spot in the neighborhood for a skillet of hot shakshuka with sweet peppers, cumin, and warm pita.

Later in the morning, I walked up through the Old Town to the Cloth Hall. Finding the entrance was confusing: the crowds in the square were all queued for the Rynek Underground, and I had to search under the exterior arcades facing St. Mary's to find the stairs up to the art gallery. I spent most of my time in front of Piotr Michałowski's work. What really blew me away was his use of negative space: instead of crowding the canvas, he left raw underpainting, open voids, and washes of smoke, using loose, thick brushwork to frame the cavalry charge in Battle of Somosierra. In the final room, I passed over the massive centerpiece canvases for the quieter, moody twilight and night landscapes, especially Józef Chełmoński's silent lakes and storm scenes. A short walk down the street brought me into the Franciscan Basilica during a Saturday afternoon wedding. Stanisław Wyspiański's massive God the Father stained glass was striking. As a Jewish traveler, seeing a physical depiction of Hashem was strange at first, and it wasn't until I noticed the sharp anatomy of the outstretched hand that the human form emerged from what initially looked like abstract swirls of water and cosmic fire. The walls throughout the nave were painted entirely with native Polish wildflowers instead of traditional church decor.

Heading toward Wawel Castle, I bought a ticket for the Dragon's Den. It really wasn't that special: a tight spiral staircase into a dimly lit limestone cave that empties out at the riverbank next to a metal dragon spitting propane flames for tourists. Worse, the one-way turnstiles meant hiking all the way back uphill to see the castle courtyards. Lunch down in Kazimierz at Yoshi Kitsune more than made up for it. When I arrived, there was one table finishing up their meal. Once they left, I had the whole restaurant to myself. The place had character, right down to the funny frog posters on the bathroom walls. The chef-owner served with genuine humility, explaining each dish and asking for feedback. The salmon uramaki melted in your mouth with a tart redcurrant mousse, and the peanut and sesame udon was full of flavor while remaining remarkably clean. After the udon, he brought over a piece of nigiri on the house, followed by the tiramiso to close out the meal. When he asked what I thought, I told him he really understands flavor and that everything was delicious. After our chat, he poured a shot of sake for each of us to share. For about thirty dollars, it was easily the best meal of the trip.

In the late afternoon, I crossed the footbridge into Podgórze to see the memorial at Plac Bohaterów Getta, with oversized bronze chairs scattered across the square. Down the street on Lwowska, I stopped at the surviving fragment of the ghetto wall, where the speculation about why it was built with rounded, tombstone-shaped arches was chilling. From there, I headed up the dirt path to Krakus Mound, an ancient pagan burial hill. Right behind it was the Liban Quarry: an overgrown limestone gorge with old fences and set pieces from Schindler's List just rusting away at the bottom. Looking south from the summit beneath a heavy autumn sky, I could see the faint, jagged silhouette of the High Tatras off in the distance. I walked back into Kazimierz for dinner at a bistro next door to my aparthotel, getting a table for the catfish fillet with morels, before finding a floor cushion at a local tea house with a pot of hot tea to wind down for the night.

entries.label: Day 13 · Oct 11
entries.title: Kraków Fortress Ring Loop Ride
text: For my final full day in Kraków, I rented a trekking bike to ride the southern ring of the Kraków Fortress trail. The city center was blocked off for the Cracovia Half Marathon. I caught the race running through the Old Town, then pedaled south to Father Bernatek Footbridge to watch the leaders sprint along the riverbank underneath. Navigating to the trail start from there was tough. I had the route on my watch, but kept doing circles before finally finding my way into the hills.

The route followed dirt tracks, wet limestone, and quiet roads connecting the old Austrian forts. I climbed up to Fort Bodzów for a view over the autumn hills, then dropped through the mud toward Fort Borek. I stopped in the courtyard there beside an old siege cannon. Further east, Fort Prokocim was completely overgrown and crumbling in the woods. By the time the trail spit me out at the river, I realized how far behind on time I was. I hammered the pedals the whole way back with GPS leading me to the aparthotel, changed out of my dirty clothes, and rushed to the museum.

Admission at the National Museum was only five złoty for their 147th birthday. After rushing to get there, it turned out I had plenty of time. I ended up seeing the whole museum with time to spare. Honestly, I thought the Cloth Hall from the day before had stronger Young Poland art. The interwar section here had some good pieces, and an 18th-century carved wooden Torah ark in the Judaica gallery stood out. I left in the late afternoon to return the bike before six, rolling across Błonia Park on the way back.

I was starving after thirty-six miles on the bike, so I started with mushroom cappellacci, dumplings, and lasagna for dinner. On the walk back, I stopped at another spot and got a red Thai curry as well. Afterward, I walked around the Old Town at night, a perspective I hadn't seen yet. The paths were quiet and very nicely maintained. From there, I headed back to my apartment in Kazimierz to pack.

entries.label: Epilogue · Oct 12
entries.title: Homeward from Kraków
text: On Monday morning, I packed my bags and walked over to the Grzegórzki station instead of trekking up to the main terminal. I stopped at a bakery for fresh bread and savory focaccia, and ended up eating it right on the platform while waiting for the train to the airport.

What started as a marathon trip to Berlin turned into two weeks moving across Central Europe by foot, train, and bike. Between twenty-six miles on the pavement in Germany, climbing along the granite ridges of the Tatras, and circling Kraków’s outer ring, it was one of the most beautiful and fun trips I’ve ever taken. Sitting at the gate waiting for the flight back to Boston, I was mostly shocked by how completely unknown this entire part of the world is in the US, and how easily I could have missed it if I hadn't taken a friend's advice. Boarding the plane to head home, I was already thinking about what was next.
